title: Naming, lived
hookLine: the family gathers, the Granth is opened, the name begins with the hukam's letter
tomorrow: why does the code say a new mother needn't wait a set number of days?

cards: A new baby in the family group chat goes the same way every time: the photo, a wall of hearts, and then one question from every aunt at once. What's her name? Simran's Bhua Preet has been dodging it for days.
Now it's Sunday, and the whole family is sitting on the gurdwara floor. The karah prashad is covered and waiting. Hymns of thanks have been sung, and Ardas said.
Bhua Preet holds the baby, and the granthi opens the Guru Granth Sahib at random. Simran's dad, Harjit, leans so far forward he almost tips over.
Because whatever sound starts the hymn on that page, the baby's name will start with it.

teach.h: THE CODE: THANKS, THEN THE GRANTH.
teach.b: This is the naming the Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, describes. Once the mother is able, the family comes to the gurdwara with karah prashad.
Hymns of thanks are sung, and the code names one by Guru Arjan on ang 396 that says, in paraphrase, the True Guru has sent this child.

teach.h: THE FIRST LETTER OF THE HYMN.
teach.b: Then the Granth is opened, a hymn is read, and the granthi proposes a name beginning with the first letter of that hymn.
A boy's name takes Singh. A girl's takes Kaur. The granthi reads.
The first letter is sassa. Bhua had a list of names on her phone, and not one starts with sassa. Then Bebe Jaswant, Simran's grandmother, says one word: Sehaj.
Calm, steady ease, a word from Gurbani. The sangat agrees. Sehaj Kaur.
Here's the part worth telling a friend tonight.

teach.h: NAAM: A NAME, AND THE NAME.
teach.b: In Punjabi, naam means a name. In Gurbani, the same word, Naam, means the Name, God's presence, remembered.
So a Sikh child's name begins inside the Name: its first sound is borrowed from the Guru's page. The parents still choose. The Guru picks where they start.
Families keep the custom in their own ways, and the code gives the shape.

how: At a Sikh naming, the family brings karah prashad to the gurdwara, hymns of thanks and Ardas are said, the Guru Granth Sahib is opened at random, and a name is chosen beginning with the first letter of the hymn; boys take Singh and girls take Kaur.

games.q: the hukam opens on a letter your family's favorite name doesn't start with. what does the custom ask?
o: open the Granth again until the letter fits the name you wanted.
find a name that starts with the hukam's letter; you still choose which.
keep the name you wanted; the letter is only a suggestion for luck.
games.why: the code has the name begin with the hymn's first letter. the family still chooses the name, starting where the Guru's page starts.

practice: Take a pen and write your own name by hand, slowly, the way you'd write it for a teacher on the first day. Then sit with what you know about it: who chose it, and why. If you don't know, let that question be the sit.
